speaker: Speaker 1
words: This is the interview with Dolly Hartman, made July 14, 1975, at Mission Point, St. Mary's, Idaho. Dale Anderson is doing the interview.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Part of it is the attitude brought about because of my involvement, both political and St. Joe's Valley Association. But I thought, I asked my headquarters if I could have a copy because I didn't want to have to strain my brain and go back in history on this. So I will make you have a copy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, fine. Can we start off with the personal data and then I can get the other thing? Maybe I should move over here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, your name.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Now, would you like my married name?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Your whole name.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My whole name.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, there's a place for your maiden name.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, all right. Well, I'm Mrs. And then I put in, quote, my nickname is Dolly. But my real name is Mae. But I go by Dolly, so I always enclose Dolly in little quote marks. And Mae, actually my name is Mae, M-A-Y Hartman. That was due to an error on the part of my grandmother who, Mae was supposed to have been my middle name and added it at my only name.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, how did that happen?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I was born, you know, in Sherwood, Wyoming, in the house. And my grandmother reported to the Bureau of Biological Statistics, and of course she reported my name and she didn't include my first name. But I have gone by Dolly all my life. Okay. And I'm also Mrs. Homer J. Hartman. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. It's somewhere. Okay, is it, do you like my word?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Would you like my first word, because I'm really not writing. Okay. One, N.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And your maiden name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: McDaniel, capital M-C, capital D-A-N-I-E-L. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Date of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: February 4th, 1924. I'm an Aquarian. If that means anything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does it mean anything to you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I, you know, I don't really believe in, you know, the preciseness of astrology, but it has been very interesting to examine what an Aquarian is supposed to be, you know, like humanitarian and all these things. And it generally, it fits, or it applies more times than it doesn't. And I get a chuckle out of it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, you said you were born in Sheridan, Wyoming. Where did you first move to Idaho?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I didn't, we didn't move to Idaho until, I moved, didn't move to Idaho until 1943.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where did you live then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Moscow, in Idaho. At Moscow, I was attending the University of Idaho.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And were you living in Sheridan before you came to Moscow?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. Would you like to have me retrace just a bit? Because I was born in Sheridan, Wyoming. We, then my parents had a homestead in southeastern Montana. And we left because of the drought. We had 640 acres, and we lived 60 miles from Sheridan. I rode horseback at the age, I was in the fourth grade, and I rode horseback to school with my little one, six-year-old sister on behind. We rode six miles a day. And this was out among the animals, from the jackrabbits. So, and we used to live in Sheridan part of the time in the wintertime, and then go out to our homestead in Decker, near Decker, and that's where all the oil is, by the way, and the oil shale is, and the coal is now. So we had a homestead in southeastern Montana. And we had an ice house in the, in a coal bank. My sister and I were going to take a trip back there this fall. I haven't been back since 35. Because we cut ice and put it up in the wintertime. Basically, I came from a family, a western family of cattle people.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that what your father did?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My father was a cattleman and rancher, and carpenter. My mother's a school, was a schoolteacher. But we were westerners, that's all they... And, so then the drought hit, and we migrated, and I was assessed, they migrate to eastern Oregon. And ours was one of the first houses on the new Vail O'ahu Irrigation Project. And so my parents were, we could consider, were new pioneers. And I graduated from Vail Union High School in Vail, Oregon, 1941. And I went to work in the shipyards during the war, and earned enough money to pay my tuition.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was that why you did that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, to go to school, I welded. And I came to, in the meantime, my parents had purchased property in Idaho. And so I arrived in Idaho before they did, and enrolled at the University of Idaho in 1943, in 1944. And I worked at the Hotel Moscow.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, did you work with Elsie Nelson?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, and I worked in the pantry and the sandwiches, and then that was mainly where I worked, was in the kitchen. I made sandwiches and salads. Is this appropriate?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, this is fine.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, okay, I'll just ramble on, so get ahead and forgive me your Idaho. And then I also worked at the knobby, and I worked at, because I had earned enough money for my tuition, but I worked on the basis of my room and board, working at these places. Then in the spring of the year, my money somewhat ran out, and it seemed appropriate to join the service. So I joined the service, I was attending the University of Idaho. I joined the WACs for two reasons. One was that I felt that when I was finished, I was going to come back and go to school under the GI Bill of Rights. And the other was I had an itching foot and an adventurous spirit, and I was assigned to the military.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you get to travel much?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, no, I was stationed two places. I was stationed in Las Vegas, Nevada, 11 months. I went from the liveliest spot on earth to the deadest spot on earth, which was Camp Chaffee, Arkansas. I flew there in the nose of a B-17.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It was a fabulous experience.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Our squadron had a squadron party planned. This was in Las Vegas, and it happened to fall on V-J night, and so we had a ringside seat for all the festivities. That was very interesting. So then I went to Camp Chaffee, Arkansas, where I was for 11 months, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And nothing happened there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, no, not really. I worked. I was a personnel clerk, and I helped organize the counseling branch at the separation center. And I did personnel work, and I was furlough and pass clerk. And I became a buck sergeant there. And we asked, and I received a meritorious achievement plaque there, because our unit, as a group, we had worked to be a meritorious achievement plaque, because we had worked above and beyond the call of duty to establish this separation center.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So I did receive that. So is that what it was, was basically a separation center?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was a separation center at Camp Chaffee. But I flew there in the nose of a B-17, and I flew over the Grand Canyon and just looked right down. I was in the nose. It was a fabulous experience. And I wouldn't give anything for the experiences I had, you know. Or even working in the shipyard.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever consider staying in the Army longer?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I did. I considered it. However, at the time I got out, because I did like it, and I did work. I was not a gold brick. And I liked working with the people. But I considered it, but the reason I decided to get out was because at that time it was not made a part of the regular Army. It was still considered an auxiliary. So I got out. And even after I got out, I did consider even going back in. Because that same year I think it did become a part of the regular Army. I was, had the war not ended, I had taken my overseas physical and as a clerk typist and a personnel clerk. Some of us were to be sent overseas. I did not sign up for overseas duty. I had three brothers who were in the service, and they said not to. So I, however, had it gone on much longer, why I wasn't going to have any, it wasn't my decision. But I had...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Why'd you go overseas? Did it appeal to you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, not really. It did not, it didn't appeal to me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was that because of the war or just the appealing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, as I said, I find myself, I don't have a, I don't have the desire to be a worldwide traveler because there's a lot here we haven't seen. I am Scotch, Irish, and English. So I would like to go to the British Isles. And I like history. So I would be interested in going to the British Isles and more or less, especially Ireland. And I have, I'm probably familiar with British and Scottish, you know, this type of history. I think I might like to go. I thought I was really going to see the nitty gritty. You see, I have to see the nitty gritty. But I can't take the heat very well. And we hosted an Indian fellow here from India. And my husband and I were both invited to come over because my husband is a graduate forester and I am a, I graduated from the University of Idaho in Dietetics, by the way. And we were invited to come over as a guest of the Indian government and, you know, and help. He said, come over for a vacation for five months and then we will pay you if you will, you know, help. I would, now I would have liked to have done that. But we couldn't leave this place for that long. But that did fascinate me. But I like to do things with a purpose, just to travel for the sake of traveling, don't feel to me too much.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That seems like a really interesting opportunity.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. I think we just have to write to this young man because he did write to several times and then I stopped writing to him. But he was from the country, or the little state of Bihar, Bihar, which is, B-I-H-A-R, which is the one that's under all this scrutiny. And he came from a family which is wealthy and he felt that the caste and class system should be, he was working to eliminate it. And he didn't have to. And his father and family and uncles were the village elders. So I know he's right in the middle of that over there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When was he here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, when I was about 19, about 5 years old. He and I moved out. That was fascinating to me. That sounded very good. Because then I wouldn't have been involved as a tourist, but I would have been involved with the people themselves. And I liked that involvement.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think you really get to know what India is about. Yes. That's great.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did I get us to Idaho yet? Yes, you got us to Idaho. I mean, we went off on a few side trips, but that was all right. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did you come to Idaho?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, how did I come? I will, okay, I will reply that you ask me that question. I had been working in the shipyards. We were frozen on the job, by the way. And that meant that we could not leave our jobs. This was during war time, in 1943. And so I applied to leave, because I wanted to go to the University of Idaho. Because my parents had purchased this property. In other words, this was going to be our home. And this was in the spring of 1943, May 1943. I climbed on a bus, Greyhound bus, in Portland, Oregon. And came by bus to Moscow. And I still can remember riding along on that bus. And I thought, this is the most beautiful country I have ever seen. Because it was green, well, a whole lot like it is now. And there were always different shades of green. And I just thought, it is just beautiful. And it did make an impression upon me. And I arrived by bus, Greyhound bus.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: At the Moscow Hotel?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I lived on, let's see, 6th Street, one of those older homes. I applied for a job. And I did get on at the Moscow Hotel. And I met Elsie Nelson, who was the one who interviewed me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We interviewed her, and in the presentation, she had them, and someone will do her part, and talking about getting the job and running the dining room at the Moscow Hotel. And then I listened to her tape, and we'd take the cassettes and put them on reel to reel. And for some reason, her tape hadn't been put on reel to reel, so I listened to that. And she just, oh, it was really interesting.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She is still with it? Mm-hmm. My goodness. She must be in her 90s.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm thinking she's in her late 80s, but I could be wrong.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She always impressed me with a very beautiful complexion. But I worked, yes, for Miss Elsie Nelson. I worked there for most of the winter. In the salads and sandwiches, and like most young people, you get to thinking that, you know, the grass is greener. And I got a little tired of it. Well, my friends decided to work somewhere else, see. But I did. I worked in the kitchen. I worked in the... Oh, I can tell you an incident about this. I worked for the salads and sandwiches. And then I also used to trap the mice for the chef. I thought this would be interesting. Because I'm not a squeamish person. I never have been. And so I think he used to give me so much extra for every mouse I had. And you used his regular traps? Yes. Uh-huh. And he always made sure I was fed very well because I was his trapper. I don't remember his name at all. That is an incident, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I lived in an apartment that in the fall the mice came in. So I put the trap in a bread sack and that's the way I got the mouse out. Because I didn't want to handle the mouse.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, at my school we handled all kinds of things. After I got through there I was a zoology lad, so I, you know, just before lunch. But anyway, yes, it was Elsie Nelson. I was employed by her. She was a fabulous lady.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I gathered that from listening to her.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Very wonderful person to work for.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Very wonderful.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I was young. I was about, I guess I was 18, going on 19, about 19. And that was really other than that shipyard work. Well, prior to that I had worked on a cattle ranch. Oh, this is an incident that might be interesting. After I graduated from out of high school my father was ill and he sold his property. And he became a guard on the dam, the Lums Springs Dam above Jantura. And while I was working in the shipyards one time I became very homesick. And I hadn't, it was eight months, I was only 18. And it was eight months between the time that I first left home and was able to come home because I developed the months and then somebody pickpocketed my $50 which I had. And so anyway, a total of eight months had passed. And I had three days that I could take off from the shipyard. This was before I quit the job to go to university. And it was about early in the spring. And I got on the bus. I worked the graveyard shift. So that meant I worked from 12 till in the morning. And so I got off that shift and climbed on the bus and headed for Jantura, Oregon. And I spent my, my folks actually were 15 miles away. 15 miles up in the hills on the Malheur River. There was the Malheur River where the dam was, which is at Beulah, Oregon. My mother was a teacher there. And my son Tony was halfway between, was about four miles from there. Well anyway, the way I had it set, and I really couldn't, it was a serious offense to be gone from your job during the war time. But I just had to go home. I hadn't been home. And so anyway, I got on that morning. And by arriving I was going to get in there at about 3 a.m. in the morning, the next morning. And I had it all arranged that I would catch the mail stage. And I would only be able to see him just a little while. And then I'd have to catch that stage back. Well I got into there, Mom had said where to knock on the door because there was a lady who I could spend the night with. Well I arrived at 3 a.m. in this little isolated town and knocked on the door and I could arouse nobody. And I had no suitcase. And I thought, well my brother walked that 15 miles, I can walk that 15 miles. Because I really didn't have that much time to spare. So I started walking. I hadn't ever been up there, but they had given me instructions. And this was quite an interesting little incident also because I knew I had 15 miles, I had my suitcase. And I've always been able to sleep anywhere. When I'm tired I still can. I can just turn off and go to sleep. So about daylight I was getting very tired. I can remember it was an early spring rain pattern on me a little bit, but that really didn't bother me any. And I thought, well it's too early for rattlesnakes. But that was rattlesnake country. In our homestead I was familiar with rattlesnakes because southeastern Montana had rattlesnakes. About daylight I guess it was I decided I was just simply tired. And I went and I had newspapers in my suitcase and I just curled up under a juniper tree down on the river. I suppose it must have been, I probably slept a couple hours. Then I woke up and trudged on with my suitcase. And it was just about 9 I guess when I got to where my saddle pony was kept. And I got my saddle pony from this fellow, this rancher. And then I put my suitcase on and rode up. Now my mother didn't know I was coming. And I arrived just as she was letting those kids out for recess. My goodness, she let out school for the whole day. And of course I broke into tears because I hadn't been home. And I was really very homesick. But I arrived by my pony and I don't know who was going to shut that mom or me. But anyway, then the whole countryside they were just astounded because somebody had seen somebody sleeping under that tree. And to think that I had walked that 15 miles. And I said well if my brother Bob could do it. And the wintertime I could do it in the summertime, in the spring. So I did and then I took the stage back. But that was a little incident that might be interesting. I don't remember those things but they come along. So that was the way I... And then after that of course I did go down to the university and I worked for the... At the hotel. I also worked at the Nest, which is now the bookstore. They used to be the Nest. They used to take salad and make short orders. So I worked my way through.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was it all your money? No help from your parents?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My parents were poor. I came from a poor family. I said we were poor in money but rich in many other things. There were nine children and eight of us were still living. And I suppose you might say we've all exceeded our economic background. But we were brought up with principles. We were brought up with honesty. We were brought up with the idea that what you own you do own. And you know these things carry on today. And we were brought up on the basis that right is might. And if you know you are right, that you stick to your gun. And so I'm... My parents were very strong people. My father's still alive. He's up there in the nursing home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where is he?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: At St. Mary's. They came from the Deadwood and Sundance, Wyoming from the days of Calamity Jane and Wild Bill Hickok and all of those. My father had a homestead a mile from the Devil's Tower. My mother was born in Deadwood, South Dakota. They had a... Life was always a struggle but we always had fun.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Adassa. Okay, what did you give me your mother's maiden name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Adassa. A-D-A-S-S-A. That was supposed to have been my name originally. But my grandmother left it off. A-D-A-S-S-A. Myrtle. Lehman.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: L-E-H?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: L-E-H-L-E-E-M-A-N. Her first husband was president... First president of the Homestead State Mining in Deadwood. She was married... Her first husband was a big cattleman and he died of cancer. And she was a widow of four children when my father married her.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, and when did they get married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Which one? My parents? My parents? My father served in World War I. They were married in Coffeyville, Kansas. The day he arrived he had her medium and he said he had a dollar in his pocket. But they were married in Coffeyville, Kansas. He traveled down to medium. What? In 19-something. They passed their 50th... It must have been 1919. They passed their 50th wedding anniversary here several years ago.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When did your mother die?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mom died a year ago. July 5th, 1974.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 59, can't believe that long.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, they've been quite senile but still a lot of their real... We've always been a very close family. I mean, while I said there were eight brothers and sisters, half of us were one family, but we were all brought up as one family. Can't tell the difference.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you know the date of your mother's birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, November 22nd, 1896.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What came your father's name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, this just slays him. Because he had to sign a affidavit to say he was a man, not a woman. His name is Mr. Hazel, H-A-Z-E-L. Ray McDaniel. Yes, he did. He had to sign an affidavit that he was a man. Why? I thought he was a woman on some form. I have a copy of it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I can appreciate how you feel.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Your data.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Dale. Dale, yes. But I've never had to go to that extreme. I mean, I had been hassled a lot. Yeah. Like, I went to pick up a check and she said, well, you need to get a note from him. I looked at it. You need to get a note from him. And then she decided, well, it was okay. And I had my ID card out there with my picture on it and finally she looked at it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: This is real funny because the office gal, that's at the nursing home, my parents were senile over a period of years and had been at the nursing home. This was after my mother had passed away, about six months after she'd passed away. And lo and behold, I end up with a Medicare card for Mrs. Hazel. I've had a terrible time with banks on this too. One place I kept getting an overdraft on them because I have power of attorney. And I kept accumulating too much in Mrs. Hazel. See, they had two bank accounts. We've had all sorts of interesting things. But anyway, the office gal up there said that the Medicare called her from Boise and said, and how is Mrs. Hazel McDaniel feeling? And she said, I just said, Mrs. Hazel McDaniel is Mr. Hazel McDaniel and Mrs. McDaniel is a DASA. And she passed away quite a few months ago. And they had, and they just said, oh, and about strangled on her. You know, in other words, they had it all in their minds that Sherry was a woman. See, they just assumed these things. And I said, but everywhere I had put Mr. M-R. And I think she's right. She said they probably thought she was a typographical error. So he was Mr. M-I-S-T-E-R. Hazel McDaniel.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did he use his middle name a lot just to help people out?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Everybody called him Mac. They still do. Oh. Yeah. No, it was Mac. H-R-A.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Today. Today is his birth.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I'll have a terrible time remembering what year. I'll have to go back. He was born April 6th. He was six and a half years younger than my mother. So she was born in 1896. Okay, he was born in 1892.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, because see, she was... Her birthday was November and his was April, so that was... She was...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, his birth.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh, Coffeyville, Kansas. It was still Oklahoma Indian Territory.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How'd they meet? Huh? How did they meet?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, that's hilarious. Um, my mother had quite a lot more education than my father. My father had just a third grade education. But he educated himself. But he worked for my grandmother, who was my mother's mother. And she ran a boarding house. And, uh, she thought really that my mother had... My father was from the wrong side of the track. And she didn't approve of the former Mrs. Henry Zimmerscheid, who had been one of these types of, you know, outstanding cattlemen. That had been my mother's first husband. And she really couldn't see my mother marrying that...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did they call him?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'll think about that. But anyway, they had a squatter from the devil's tower. They definitely were not of the same... In my grandmother's eyes, they definitely were not on the same social standing. And so she... He worked for my grandmother. And that's where I met my mother. And he wanted her to marry him before she... He went overseas and she told him no, because she was older than he was. And yet she had these four children. And so... But if he still, you know, cared to... They'd wait and see. And so she met him and they got married the day he arrived in the state.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Your mother was older than your father? Then when was her estate being 1990?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Six. Well, she was 1886.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, 86. I got 96.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no, she was 1886.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, okay. Everything makes sense now. Yeah. Okay. Okay. Your brothers and sisters.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, wow. You brought us over here three hours. Well, let me start out with just the names. Well, my older brother, Ted Zimmerscheid. He's a half-brother.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How do you spell Zimmerscheid?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Z-I-M-M-E-R S-C-H-I-E-D And he fought with Merrill Smaragders in World War II. But he passed away. He's deceased. And he was born in... He would have been 68 this year.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I just need to know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Then a sister, June Moskal. It was June Zimmerscheid Moskal. M-O-S-K-A-L She's an artist.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She later retired during McCook, Nebraska, but she paints India. She painted a picture for the Indian Center in Spokane. The one that says, The Race of Sorrows. That's her painting. And then I have a brother. So she's from Nebraska. Then I have a brother, Kenneth Zimmerscheid. And he is in Vail, Oregon. You don't want to know where they are?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was just asking about her because she was an artist. Yeah, okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Then I have a half-brother, Carl Zimmerscheid. And he is in Texas.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Texas.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Then my older brother of the McDaniels is Robert R. McDaniels. And he, well I guess just recently is in Kenilworth, Washington.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They were just transferred.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He's a graduate of WSU. Any rivalry? What? Any rivalry between you? No, he started out in Oregon State. He was an old fellow when he graduated too. I didn't graduate until 1954. Then I have a sister, Betty. And that's Mrs. Galen Klein in Tucson, Arizona. And then I have a sister, Mrs. Jo Minglecamp. Moscow, Idaho.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Minglecamp?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: M-E-N-G-E-L-K-E-M-P. There's a lot of them around Moscow. And then I have an unmarried sister.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What was her first name? Helen.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Then I have an unmarried sister, Peggy. Her real name's Eleanor, but Peggy includes. McDaniels. And she's in Missoula, Montana.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you know why she never got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was her own choosing. She said that she was too independent. She liked to be able to do what she wishes to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was she ever hassled about not getting married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not within our family. Because we believed greatly. By the way, we had many religions in our family. We were brought up to respect the rights of others, and that includes our own family. And if she's hassled, and this is within our family that she's hassled, she chooses to be single. And she's in her forties. She doesn't intend to get married. She likes to lead her own life and make her own decisions. Okay, your husband's name is Homer J. Hartman. Homer Jackson Hartman. He's from Jackson County, Oregon.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that where he was born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's where he was born. He was born in Jacksonville.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The date of his birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have a terrible time on this. September 28th. This is 75. So 15 take away 8 is 1907.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And the date and place you were married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Moscow, Idaho.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you meet him while going to school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. I met him while I worked for the Forest Service. I was a cook in the blister rust camp. I had 50 college kids when I was first cook. And he was one of the bosses.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you remember mentioning that in your courtship?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, yes, because I married one of the bosses. He was the bachelor of the woods. So we kept it a secret that we were going together. There really weren't many places we could go. I remember I would... because I only had one day off. So we would just meet up sometimes in the woods. And so I can still remember one of the camp bosses said, Don't know the old potato farmer. Are you meeting down the road? And I just laughed, you know, because it was one of his bosses, you know. And I just laughed and I said, well, you'll be surprised. So then we were engaged to be married. We were married in September. And yes, I can, because we felt that I had been quite outspoken and was one of the bosses. He was a little bit outspoken. And we felt that all of his friends and my friends would assume that we were going to get married on Labor Day. And so I just went to work as usual on Labor Day. And then we were married on September 11th. And because we felt that we would, we might have got the ceremony over with, but we'd have probably been on different forests before it was all over with. So anyway, we were engaged and he gave me my diamond in August of that year. So then everybody became general knowledge. That was 19. He was my second husband. And people used to say, well, now how did he, how did you catch him? And I said, many cooks have tried. And I said, well, I wasn't trying. Because I had decided I was going to school. I was going to school under the G.I. Bill Bright. And I really didn't have time to be bothered with men. Because I had a young son I was helping, you know, raising too. Plus the fact that I was taking a dietetics course, which was very rugged. Especially if I had never, since I had never had algebra. And I really didn't have time to be bothered with men. And I had decided to be a career woman. And so I said I didn't try to catch him. He caught me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long did you know him before you got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I knew him two years. Because he was a boss. I had worked out there first. I worked out there, I started to work as a flunky in the Forest Service in 1951 when I started the school. The second time. See, I went to school in 43 and 44. Then I went into the service. And I was in the service two years. And then I was married and I split up with this other husband and I had a small son. And so I had to, I decided I was the lady veteran. I used to always louse them up at the registrar's office because I was, they didn't expect me to be a, you know, the women veteran at that time. So when I started to school, there had been seven years and a lot of water under the bridge. And I tackled the dietetics course. I lived at Vets Village Farm. And my parents took care of my son, Steve, and I used to do all my studying in four days. See, I really didn't have time to be involved. And then I would go out and work because my father's health was never too good. So I used to go out to the farm and help. And I can, you might be interested, before I went to school, the year of 48 and 49 was big snows. And my sister, and that was my first year when I had come back from leaving my other husband. And it was out of necessity and I don't care to go in to it. But my father had had an accident and so he babysat Stephen. And my sister Peggy and I, my mother taught school and she skied across, there was huge snows, and she skied across to catch the bus to teach. And my sister Peggy and I spent all winter just simply melting snow to water a cow and for family use. And in order to melt it, we had to sell the wood. And we had gotten much wood in but the snows came early. And we didn't have enough for the winter. And we had an old broken down barn and we had no tractor. And I could, I would go out and climb up on that barn and with a crosscut saw, saw down portions of that barn and we saw the log of the time to burn. And she had to stay on the beaten tractor because the snow was so terribly deep. And so we had many ropes. Two guys who didn't have pictures of this. Because I would sit up there, straddle the canopy and saw with a crosscut and then attach a rope to it. And then she'd be way off somewhere and would pull this log over to the saw we had. And that was the way we got through the winter of 48, 49. And my mother who was 60, in her 60s, skiing across the field to go. So we've been a somewhat self-reliant family.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's just so good. Oh wow. Yeah, I mean, this has been a lot of, a very fine experience.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because all they did, they made us stronger. They didn't, we weren't ever weakened by them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I say that's fascinating.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But we spent our full time. There was a cycle. We would get, would gather snow, melt snow, you know, water the cows, wash the diapers. And my father was bedridden, but he babysat my young son who was, let's see, he was about a year old at that time. But my sister and I did that. Well, yes, I don't believe I would give anything for those experiences.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh wow. Your husband's occupation was job, Forest Service? Yes, he was, he left Forest Service.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And he was tired. I better turn off the oven. I will have dried up.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have any interest, hobbies, and talents other than what you do?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes I do. First of all, my first hobby I would say is people, and I suppose it is helping people to help themselves. Now when I say just helping people, I don't like to approach it from the point of view of like putting Sam on a couch. I mean I feel that I help people by helping them to, working with the strength of people to make them, I like to deal with the positives. Oh yes, I cook. I like to cook. I'm a creative cook. And I do sourdough cooking. I make wine. Just recently, now I am working with this Indian girl. And we are, together we are doing a self-determined 4-H project. She was interested in conservation of her Indian culture. And she had this book and she said, see the Coeur d'Alene's were in this area. And I'm also interested in history. And so she was interested in finding out about the foods that they use, the plants they use. So I said, I approached the county agent and I said I would like to suggest that this is what we would like to do. And we would, so we started out with foods this year. And her mother is my assistant leader. And she is teaching loon weaving and what not. We had just a small group of us there, six of us, six groups, six children. And we're having a lot of fun. But we put on, Michael Parker and her mother Deanna and I put on four one-hour sessions for the combined, for the 4-H camp. And it was, we had parts of Indian cookery and wild foods. In fact, I've got a book here. And I was so busy acknowledging everybody that I forgot to put on this book that it was produced by me. But I've got everybody else's. Produced by me in cooperation with the county agent's office. But anyway, I like to cook, but not just, it's creative cooking. I do all kinds of cooking. And, I like horseback riding. I like reading. And I'm good to write. If I ever get rid of this Forest Service thing and the Wild and Scenic Rivers thing, that will be decided by 1976. That has taken too much of my time. But I wish to do some writing. But I definitely like to read. And then I suppose my other interest is really serving. This is an era of councils, commissions, and, oh, and I have two seats. Councils, commissions, and committees. And one person can influence a great deal sitting on some of these committees. And they mainly deal with federal funding. And so I have spent much time, as you read my biography, I became involved in comprehensive health planning. And I've gotten right in the middle of the thing. And I helped put the bylaws together and I chaired up the personnel policy. Because if the right people don't get involved, the wrong people will be. So this is a lot of my involvement. And I really am sometimes spread pretty thin. But then you get some know-how. So I have served on, I feel that councils and commissions and committees are essential components of this federal funding. I would like to see less federal funding. I would like to see less federal involvement. But since it is here in Wilkerson, I believe that responsible people shouldn't bury their head in the sand. They should become a part of this thing. And then they can keep them level and stabilized. And I sit on the health facilities review board, the state board. I go to Boise once a month. And there are nine of us. And the last meeting we chose between the hometown boy, who had it all hanging out, his honesty and his limitations. But also what was hanging out was his love for the people. As compared to the corporation that had everything down pat. Well, we chose the hometown boy. By choosing, we, this board that I sit on, health facilities review board, we review all applications for health facilities. That's nursing homes, hospitals, big equipment. Involving expenditures, $100,000 or more. Is that state money? Well, it's federal funds. And see, this is the thing. We do not have a certificate of need legislation in the state of Idaho. The state of Idaho is moving towards moving these state people out of state institutions. And putting them in specialized shelters out in communities. So right now it appears as though it is good business. You know, they have nothing to lose. These operators have nothing to lose at the present time. Because they are, they have a cost reimbursement thing from the state if they become a nursing home or facility. So it's very important that we set up criteria and standards because we feel that the service to these people is the primary thing. So we, it's interesting too. And I go to Boise once a month. But it isn't as difficult as it sounds because I can absorb a lot in a hurry. And I fly in and I usually have, I take my homework with me. Lock myself up in a motel room so that I don't get out and just talking to people. Oh. That's where I discipline myself. Lock myself up in a motel room and do my homework.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Learn about all the things, right? Yeah. You have on that sheet of paper all your awards and honors and things like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well I have two that I haven't got on there that I should have. Yes, I do. Except I have some additions and one was I received, I received a plaque from, as a result I did disaster work at Pomeroy. And I received an award from, signed by Governor Evans. I was the on-site director of Pomeroy, Washington during that flood. And this was I had volunteered, you understand. And it takes a matter of about two months to work one of these out and I'd go back. And anyway I did receive an award signed by Governor Evans and the head of the civil, state, Washington Civil Defense. And then I received an award from the Department of Civil Defense, Department of the Army for the Pomeroy, Pomeroy work. And the reason I'm in Washington, you see I am a volunteer disaster consultant for the Inland Empire Division which covers parts of Idaho and Washington. And Florida, do we have more than enough? No, Idaho and Washington. And there's five, see we have 11 northern counties in Idaho. And the, well, clear the Yakima on that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What is the San Jose Valley Association doing as far as trying to, are you just working against the Walden City Rivers Act?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we were working against the, it's too bad you have to use negative things to, for a positive approach. We are a group of several hundred land owners. And our aim is to, is actually protect our private rights as private owners. Now, we have layers of, we are threatened by several layers of federal government in this valley. One is the Forest Service under the Walden City Rivers Act, and that would be management. Also, one of the things that bothers us is the Forest Service has conducted the study, so they have done the studiers. They have developed the criteria by which the study is conducted. And then there will be the managers. Now, I don't feel that is objective. How can you be objective? And there has been no economic impact statement. There is an environmental impact statement in the bill, but there has not been an economic impact study done. As to what it will cost.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, the environmental statement hasn't been completed there, has it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, the environmental statement, they tell me, I have a very hard time, it's lost somewhere in the, it is in the mill. I understand the environmental draft statement is in Missoula, the regional office. We will be monitoring it. I'll keep it monitored. I understand the problem.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you have to say about the offspring?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have not seen it. This is a carefully guarded secret. Kept in a secret by the Forest Service. They tell me that it will, that these impact studies will be made available to everybody at once after it's filed in the Federal Register. But that means there will be so many layers at a level that it's gone through for approval before we ever get the chance to look at it and challenge it. But challenging it we will. I'm sure there's many things in there, but so far we've challenged them. One of the things that we think will be real interesting is to see how the Forest Service reconciles, and this isn't something I'm taking off the top of my head, that at their hearings and the input, the people against classification greatly outnumbered those that were for it. We know it, and not one hearing but both hearings. In the beginning you see probably 90% of the valley is against classification. So then they had, the Forest Service said, but we have to, this is a national concern, we have to get people's input nationally. So while they were busy we were developing our own public, and we have a national public too. While we have several hundred members, we have several thousand people on a mailing list. And we then went to work and we got input from, we had 20 states, about 20 states. And then we had a cross section of people that wrote to the Forest Service. So we went to work and we developed a national public too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there any alternative plans that you've developed?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we feel there should be no classification, and the reason is, I'm going to dig you out of my latest little thing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Time veteran alternatives, if you have one.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, okay. All of the reasons originally, three years ago, and the environmentalists said, you know, development on the flood plain, flood plain, you know, this was the big reason. But they had to have the Swanson River Act implemented. Well now, as a result of the floods, we have a federal agency in here with flood plain zoning. These flood plains are under the Federal Disaster Protection Act of 1973, and it's administrated by HUD.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What does that mean?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That restricts the type of buildings and what can be done on the flood plain. It has to be flood proofed if they have any, which is very costly. We also have the State Department of Health, and they are responsible for the quality of water. And they have set forth some very great restrictions. And so, between those two, that is taking care of the reasons that the environmentalists were talking about a vigilance.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It actually is preventing the development.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, yes. And cleaning up the existing. Now, there isn't too much pollution out here. Yes, there's some pollution. But we caught, and this year we had a bumper number of cutthroat trout right out here in front.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's insane, you go fishing out here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm not much of a fisherman. I let them bring them to me and I cook them. I like to fish, but I'm busy doing other things. And we've had a real good season of fishing, and many of them cutthroat trout. Cutthroat trout are the first thing to die out in a polluted area. So you see, I can't buy this big pollution thing that they're hollering about. I've eaten the cutthroat trout, but I've eaten their spring. And now the Health Department is getting with it, and they are enforcing the water quality codes. And the county billing permits are required as a result of this HUD. So what reason then would you have? The reason is, it's a federal land grant, it's a public land grant. And I really feel that the environmental concern is very secondary. That it is for a big recreational boom, which will overuse the river. And I think that they're using the environment, it's under the guise of environmental concern. It's a big recreational boom, which is all right if they want to go to route everybody else and purchase property or lease it or whatever. But just to decide by public decree, you know, eminent domain, why? I can pay the taxes and still be liable and still not do what I can do on my own property, and that's what I'm after. So I have made a little personal pledge to myself. I have learned a lot, personally, in these three years. I'm able to talk, and I'm able to write. And people will listen. And I just have made a little pledge that I will spend, I can't think of any better way to spend the rest of my life than sticking out my feet and letting the Empire's builders and the bureaucracy stumble over me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And that's what I'm after.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because I have nothing, you know, I have nothing to lose anyway. This is going to be a very small finish yet by any means. One of the things I hope to do, the Reader's Digest, and this is in the back, working from the mind. The Reader's Digest, several years ago, wrote about the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act and what a great thing it was. And I thought it would be good to try for one of those first-person awards to write, now this is the other side of the coin, from a point of view as president of this organization, and point out some of the fallacies.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that the Bill of Rights for the Rivers? I've seen that, Reader's Digest, but I don't know if that's it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, that isn't it. It has to do with the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act. But I think I could put together one. That's some toys with that too. I have to get all my canning out of the way, I'll do that maybe this winter.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you freeze things too?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes, I freeze in my can.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you want anything?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do I dry? I have a dehydrator and I make jerky.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I'd like to see your dehydrator.

words: Let me bring it up.
